analysis.explanation: The Random Forest scores this binary as malware at 0.925, and all 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking (individual SHAP +0.005 to +0.011). Two groups of patterns fit cryptographic or hashing code. The first is rotate-heavy code: MOV ROL (rank 1, +0.010575, highest frequency at 0.002687), MOVZX ROL (+0.007081) and ROL ADD (+0.005329). The second is multi-word carry arithmetic: SUB SBB (+0.009985), SUB ADC (+0.007132), MOV ADC (+0.005514), ADD ADC (+0.005295) and MOV SHRD (+0.005296). Rotations and carry chains are typical of hash rounds and big-integer math, which mining algorithms use. A second group of n-grams, PUSH RET (+0.009387), POP PUSH (+0.008157), CALL PUSH, XOR PUSH, ADD PUSH, ADD POP, PUSH AND and CALL ADD, reflects stack-heavy control flow and calling-convention glue. This could point to obfuscation, packing or a stack-based dispatcher, but it is also common in ordinary compiled code. Several of these n-grams are very rare (about 0.000168 to 0.001 relative frequency), and no function-level locations or observed behaviors are attached to any of them. Rotation and ADC/SBB/SHRD sequences also occur in benign crypto, compression and bignum libraries, so they do not by themselves separate a miner from legitimate cryptographic code. CMOVZ MOV has frequency 0.000000 yet contributes +0.005640, so its influence comes from the model's learned absence or presence pattern rather than an observable code feature. The evidence is consistent with cryptojacking and the model's confidence is high, but without function attribution or mining-specific indicators it is not conclusive. I classify it as low-confidence, leaning malicious.
